newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO split on progress of talks.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO split on progress of talks.

text.p: Palestinians and Israelis split sharply on Monday whether talks on a long-delayed Israeli redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron had achieved progress.
"There are a lot of difficulties, they are not intending to implement accurately and honestly what had been agreed upon and what had been signed," Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said in Jordan.

A senior aide to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, sounded a positive note: "Progress has been made. Things look good, things look promising," the adviser, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.

Negotiators and diplomats battled in Jerusalem and Amman to break an impasse over the Hebron pullback while the fate of formal U.S.-brokered talks slated for Tuesday in Egypt's Red Sea resort of Taba remained unclear.

Palestinian chief negotiator Saeb Erekat, holding informal talks with Israeli counterpart Lieutenant-General Dan Shomron at a Jerusalem hotel Monday, said Israel's desire to modify the Hebron accord would deal a "total knockout" to the deal agreed to by Israel's previous government.

"Mr Netanyahu insists on opening the agreement. He wants for instance the right of Israeli troops to enter Hebron, or "hot pursuit'. That is a total knockout to the agreement," Erekat told Israeli Channel One television.
Netanyahu seeks modifications in the Hebron deal in order to safeguard 400 Jews living in heavily-armed compounds amidst 100,000 Palestinians in Hebron.
U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross rushed to Amman, where Arafat held talks with Jordan's King Hussein earlier on Monday, to try to bridge the gap between the sides.
Hussein was due to travel with Arafat on Tuesday to self-ruled Jericho in the West Bank, his first trip to the territory since Israel seized it from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East war.
Jordan state television said King Hussein, in a telephone call to Netanyahu, stressed "the need to continue with the peace process and exert efforts to overcome obstacles facing it".
King Hussein, Israel's closest Arab ally since Jordan signed a peace treaty in 1994, has stepped up public support of Arafat in recent days while distancing himself from Netanyahu.

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said that barring a last-minute retreat in positions, a deal was close with the PLO on the long-promised Hebron redeployment. "It's not a matter of weeks but perhaps a number of days...but there are additional issues facing us," Levy told parliament.
Earlier Netanyahu said he would meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat when a Hebron deal was near. Netanyahu's office said late on Monday the meeting would not take place on Tuesday.

Senior Arafat aide Khaled Salam told Reuters the Palestinian leader had instructed PLO negotiators to travel to Taba on Tuesday for the formal U.S.-mediated talks, but it was not immediately clear whether the Israeli team would meet them there.

"The Palestinian delegation...has received urgent instructions from President Arafat to travel tonight to Taba," Salam told Reuters. "These instructions are in line with Palestinian commitments to the agreement with the Israeli and American sides that talks would start on Tuesday."
The formal Taba talks were to have resumed on Monday but were pushed back to allow the sides to progress in informal negotiation channels.
Salam said Israel sought to change the venue of the talks.
"We are simply looking where it is better and more comfortable to continue the talks," Shomron told Israel television.

In Cairo, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said he had received assurances from Israeli President Ezer Weizman, in Egypt to mend fences with Israel's powerful Arab neighbour, that Israel would honour signed commitments.
"The president (Weizman) assured me that they are honouring the agreements and it is going to be implemented," Mubarak told a joint news conference with the Israeli head of state.
But Mubarak refused to meet Netanyahu until the right-wing leader agreed to implement the Hebron pullback, which has become the Arab litmus test of Netanyahu's intentions on peace.
